title: They should make a play about this tbh #alecbaldwin #shialabeouf #bro...
transcript: The beef between Shia Labeouf and Alec Baldwin was like the Godzilla vs. Kong of messy, volatile Hollywood stars. And it all surrounded an ill-fated Broadway play. Welcome to another episode of Overthinking Theatre Throwback, where I do retrospectives on recent theatre history. In late 2012, it was announced that Alec Baldwin and Shia Labeouf were going to star alongside Tom Sturridge in a revival of the 1983 play Orphans by Kyle Kessler. A play about two orphan brothers who kidnap a businessman. For context, both of these actors were somewhere in the middle of their tumultuous relationship with the public eye. LaBeouf had already been arrested multiple times and Baldwin had his own history of hot tempered altercations. But both of them were years away from what would become, respectively, their most damning public incidents to date. But we're here back in February of 2013, where only a week into rehearsals, it was announced that Shia Labeouf would be departing this Broadway production due to creative differences. But things were only just starting to get messy. Later that same evening, following the announcement of his departure, Labeouf began leaking private emails between him, Alec Baldwin and the director Daniel Sullivan, and it seemed at first to reveal that there were no hard feelings. After a somewhat poetic speech about his troubled upbringing, LaBeouf said “A man can tell you he was wrong,” “that he did wrong. He can tell you when he is lost…” “He can apologize, even if sometimes it's just To put an end to the bickering,” “Alec, I’m sorry for my part in the disagreeable situation.” LaBeouf seemed to forward this email to the rest of the team, and the director, Daniel Sullivan, replied, “I'm too old for disagreeable situations.” “You’re one hell of a great actor.” “Alec is who he is. You are who you are.” “You two are incompatible. I should have known it.” “This one will haunt me. You tried to warn me.” “You said you were a different breed. I didn't get it.” And Baldwin's pretty gracious reply ended with, “I don't have an unkind word to say about you. You have my word.” But only a couple weeks later, LaBeouf started leaking more private emails, revealing more about the nature of the conflict. Baldwin has said, “we start Monday, but I'm so fking tired.” LaBeouf responded, “I'm a Hustler, I don't get tired.” “I'm 26, Chief.” Baldwin responded, “listen, boy,I'm not your fking chief.” “You got that? Ha ha ha ha ha ha ha! Let's go.” Sullivan responds to LaBeouf privately, “I think he's nervous.” Then after the first day of rehearsal, said, “I thought it was a good first day,” “even if Alec never looked up,” meaning from his script. Baldwin's only comment at the time was to say that he was “disappointed” about the email leak, though he would have more to say later. Notably, this was not the first time that an actor departed a Broadway production because of a conflict with Alec Baldwin. It happened only seven years earlier with the late, great Jan Maxwell. In any case, it was announced that the actor Ben Foster would be replacing Shia Labeouf. The production went on and in a very dramatic move, Shia Labeouf attended the first performance from the front row. The production got two Tony nominations, one for Best Revival, and the only actor to be nominated was the third one, Tom Sturridge, who hasn't even really been involved in this drama. But the production closed early due to poor ticket sales. We would still go on to learn a lot more about what happened, both from Baldwin and LaBeouf’s perspectives. Over the next year, Alec Baldwin was mired in other sorts of controversy, and a full year after the Orphans drama, Vulture published a tell-all essay that he wrote entitled “Goodbye Public Life.” It's extremely long and bizarre, covering a wide range of topics, defending himself from the accusations of homophobia, talking about his conflicts with the CEO of MSNBC and the paparazzi, and ending with a long lament about how New York has changed and the media has changed, which is not devoid of good points but does have a bit of an “old man yells at cloud” energy. And of course he gets into the Orphans drama. He said about LaBeouf, “I'd heard from other people he was potentially very difficult to work with,” “but I always ignore that because people say the same Thing about me.” “He had Learned all his lines in advance,” “even emailing me videos in which he read aloud his lines from the entire play” “to prove that he had put in the time.” “One day, he attacked me in front of everyone.” “He said, ‘you're slowing me down.’” “‘You don't even know your lines.’” “‘And if you don't say your lines, I'm just going to keep saying my lines.’” Baldwin responds “If I don't say my words fast enough,” “you're going to just say your next line?” “You realize the lines are written in a certain order?” And when it became clear that the two couldn't work together, interestingly, Baldwin offered to quit, but the producers said no, and they chose to fire LaBeouf instead. He then took shots at the director, Daniel Sullivan, for playing both sides and not being that invested. In that same intervening year, LaBeouf also had his share of additional controversies, one of which was also Broadway related. He got arrested at a performance of Cabaret for drunken behavior. But he spoke to Interview Magazine about the Orphans situation, owning up to a lot of troubling behavior. He essentially corroborates Baldwin's story and gives us yet more evidence why method acting is terrible. “I came in method. I was sleeping in the park.” “I'd wake up, walk to rehearsals.” “I was so scared to do the play” “that I had memorized it before ever coming to rehearsal.” “And my whole goal was to intimidate the fk out of Baldwin.” And even after getting fired, “I stayed in New York for a month.” “I was following him home. I was completely broken.” “And still in character.” But he does mention a couple times in this interview that he made peace with Baldwin, thus putting to bed one of the messiest public incidents in recent Broadway memory.
classificationReason: A retrospective on the behind-the-scenes drama surrounding the 2013 Broadway production of 'Orphans' (the Shia LaBeouf/Alec Baldwin conflict). Not a first-hand review of a production attended; it's a historical commentary piece. 'Orphans' is not on the provided show list.
